Theme

Time, the calendar & feasts · Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

suddenly adverb

also all of a sudden, all at once, unexpectedly

classical

Plaut. Amph. 1062: ut subitō, ut properē, ut validē tonuit!
Ter. Ph. 180: ita nunc imparātum subitō tanta tē impendent mala
Traupman 387: suddenly, statim, subitō, repente

subitō

adverb

suddenly, all of a sudden

The everyday word, in comedy and in prose (Lewis & Short: frequent and classical).

Other words

  • 1repente: short final e (Lewis & Short rĕpentē, against its own dērepentĕ). Verg. A. 2.380, trepidusque repente refugit: the fifth foot, -pente re-, is a dactyl; so Verg. A. 2.465 and 7.27, Lucr. 6.667, Ov. Met. 4.402, Juv. 2.83. The ablative of repēns, with the short -e of the third declension; de Vaan 520, s.v. repēns, prints repente.

    repente1 — suddenly, all at once

    adverb · also used · classical · Liv. 7.26.3: corvus repente in galeā cōnsēdit; Caes. BG 1.52.3: hostēs repente celeriterque prōcurrērunt; Traupman 387

  • dē imprōvīsō (ex imprōvīsō) — unexpectedly, without warning

    adverbial phrase · also used · classical · Caes. BG 2.3.1: eō cum dē imprōvīsō celeriusque omnium opīniōne vēnisset; Plaut. Rud. 1192: quī ex imprōvīsō fīliam invēnī meam?

    What no one saw coming, rather than what happens in a flash.

Examples

  • subitō nōbīs hodiē Alexandrīnae nāvēs appāruērunt

    suddenly today the ships from Alexandria came into viewSen. Ep. 77.1

  • ut subitō, ut properē, ut validē tonuit!

    how suddenly, how fast, how loud it thundered!Plaut. Amph. 1062

  • namque cōnserentī jam manum Rōmānō corvus repente in galeā cōnsēdit, in hostem versus

    for just as the Roman closed with him, a raven suddenly landed on his helmet, facing the enemyLiv. 7.26.3

See also at once, quickly, sudden.
